definition: A vision-guided robot (VGR) system is a robot fitted with one or more cameras used as sensors to provide a secondary feedback signal to the robot controller for a more accurate movement to a variable target position.
details: VGR enables robots to be adaptable and more easily implemented, while reducing the cost and complexity of fixed tooling previously associated with the design and set up of robotic cells, including material handling, automated assembly, agricultural applications, and life sciences. Vision-guided robotics can be economically advantageous in countries with high manufacturing overheads and skilled labor costs by reducing manual intervention, improving safety, increasing quality, and raising productivity rates. The expansion of vision-guided robotic systems is part of the broader growth within the machine vision market, which is expected to grow to $17.72 billion by 2028. This growth can be attributed to the increasing demand for automation and precision, as well as the broad adoption of smart technologies across industries.

explainer.lead: A vision-guided robot is fitted with one or more cameras whose output feeds the controller as a secondary feedback signal for more accurate movement to a variable target position. It matters because it makes robots adaptable and cheaper to deploy by reducing the need for fixed tooling.

tiers.eli5: Instead of moving to a spot fixed in advance, the robot looks with a camera and adjusts to where the target actually is.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use camera feedback to locate variable targets in material handling, assembly, agriculture and life sciences. A pitfall is relying on the camera signal as secondary feedback without accounting for its accuracy relative to the controller's needs.
tiers.paperLevel: A VGR system is defined as a robot with one or more cameras used as sensors providing a secondary feedback signal to the robot controller for more accurate movement to a variable target position. Its stated benefits are adaptability, easier implementation, and reduced cost and complexity versus fixed tooling.

explainer.example: In automated assembly, a robot with a camera adjusts its movement to the actual position of a part presented at a variable location instead of a fixed jig position.
